question: Who is held directly accountable under the law for the medication decisions made during clinical care?
explanation: The practitioner who administers the medication bears direct legal accountability for that clinical action. [learn more](BMP127_U3_T3#BMP127_U3_T3_h1)

question: Why can a midwife not rely on an informal hospital verbal habit to justify giving an unprescribed medication?

options.A: Verbal orders are completely illegal in all clinical settings worldwide
options.B: Statutory council boundaries and professional accountability override informal facility habits
options.C: Midwives are legally classified as independent retail pharmacists
options.D: Hospitals never keep written records of verbal instructions given to staff

explanation: Regulatory standards require every practitioner to operate strictly within approved legal and professional scopes, regardless of facility habits. [learn more](BMP127_U3_T3#BMP127_U3_T3_h1)

question: How many times should a midwife check the prescription label against the drug chart during administration?
explanation: Standard safety checks involve verifying the medication label multiple times before giving the drug to catch any mistakes early. [learn more](BMP127_U3_T3#BMP127_U3_T3_h2)

question: Why is recording a medication administration before actually giving it considered a major legal breach?

options.A: It falsifies the medical record and removes the truthfulness of the clinical timeline
options.B: It wastes valuable paper in the patient file
options.C: It automatically increases the cost of the drug
options.D: It slows down the pharmacy restocking process

explanation: Documentation must always reflect real-time events. Recording early misrepresents the actual sequence of patient care. [learn more](BMP127_U3_T3#BMP127_U3_T3_h2)

question: What legal concept requires a midwife to follow a standard of reasonable care to prevent patient harm?
explanation: Duty of care is the fundamental legal obligation to protect patients from foreseeable injury through competent practice. [learn more](BMP127_U3_T3#BMP127_U3_T3_h3)

question: A midwife gives a restricted drug outside her approved professional list. What is the main legal risk?

options.A: She is exempted from all future civil lawsuits regarding that patient
options.B: She automatically gains full medical officer status in that facility
options.C: She breaches her scope of practice, making her vulnerable to severe negligence claims if harm occurs
options.D: She transfers legal liability entirely to the hospital gatekeeper

explanation: Operating outside defined professional boundaries removes legal protection and exposes the practitioner to liability if the patient is harmed. [learn more](BMP127_U3_T3#BMP127_U3_T3_h3)

question: What is the correct way to fix a written mistake on a paper clinical record?

options.A: Tear out the entire page and rewrite the complete nursing note
options.B: Use a bottle of liquid correction fluid to completely cover the mistake
options.C: Scratch out the incorrect word heavily until it is completely unreadable
options.D: Draw a single neat line through the error, write the correction, and sign beside it

explanation: Drawing a single line keeps the original entry visible while showing the correction clearly, which prevents any suspicion of record tampering. [learn more](BMP127_U3_T3#BMP127_U3_T3_h4)

question: Which of the following examples shows objective and legally sound clinical documentation?

options.A: Patient was uncooperative and complaining about everything
options.B: Patient refused to take her prescribed medication because she is stubborn
options.C: Patient looked very tired and miserable all through the morning shift
options.D: Patient grimaced and clutched her lower abdomen during contractions

explanation: Objective notes record observable physical actions and signs without adding personal judgments about the patient's attitude. [learn more](BMP127_U3_T3#BMP127_U3_T3_h4)

question: What is the immediate priority when a midwife discovers that a medication error has happened?

options.A: Blame the junior student on duty for the mistake
options.B: Assess the patient and notify the attending physician
options.C: Resign immediately from the clinical post
options.D: Hide the medication chart in a private locker

explanation: Checking the patient's condition and notifying the medical team immediately are vital to address any potential harm. [learn more](BMP127_U3_T3#BMP127_U3_T3_h5)

question: Why is altering a patient record after realizing a medication error happened legally dangerous?

options.A: It has no legal consequence if nobody noticed the change
options.B: It prevents the pharmacy from ordering replacement drugs
options.C: It automatically lowers the hospital electricity bill
options.D: It turns a clinical mistake into a deliberate act of falsification and fraud

explanation: Covering up an error by tampering with records destroys professional trust and creates serious criminal liability. [learn more](BMP127_U3_T3#BMP127_U3_T3_h5)

question: What must a midwife do when a competent patient legally refuses a prescribed medication?

options.A: Document the refusal, explain the risks, inform the supervisor, and record witness signatures
options.B: Force the medication into the patient because staff know what is best
options.C: Call the local security guards to restrain the patient immediately
options.D: Throw away the patient case notes and discharge her without paperwork

explanation: Respecting patient autonomy involves explaining risks, notifying supervisors, and keeping a thorough record to protect everyone involved. [learn more](BMP127_U3_T3#BMP127_U3_T3_h6)

question: Which action is NOT legally acceptable when dealing with a patient who refuses treatment?

options.A: Documenting the exact conversation in the official case notes
options.B: Forcing the treatment upon the patient without their agreement
options.C: Explaining the potential health risks of refusing the drug
options.D: Informing the supervising medical officer about the refusal

explanation: Administering treatment against a competent adult's refusal is considered battery and violates legal and human rights. [learn more](BMP127_U3_T3#BMP127_U3_T3_h6)
